cim_eredeti: Interview Sofia Romansky | Strategies, Approaches and Critical Lenses to Use and Manage AI with Integrity
szoveg_eredeti:
Making Integrity Tangible in a Digital Age: Concrete Practices, Insights, and Reflections for Fostering Integrity in Professional Settings.

Sofia Romansky: There are many dimensions to consider. First, it is important to note that artificial intelligence in institutions across all sectors is not new. Various forms of artificial intelligence, including intelligent algorithms, have been used already for many years. But the attention that we are currently paying to artificial intelligence comes from a specific subcategory of the technology, which is generative artificial intelligence. For background and clarity, generative artificial intelligence at the highest level can be defined as a model that can, with various degrees of autonomy, process a particular input and based on the input cues, create some kind of output. This technology, as it is right now, is a probabilistic system, meaning that the modification from input to output happens based on a certain subset of training data. And these elements, the training data, the input, and the output, are all related to how integrity can be challenged.

As for the first element, the training data, we must acknowledge that humans are incredibly biased creatures. But that is not necessarily a problem. Bias and heuristics are things that have helped us survive throughout our evolutionary history. It is a feature of our biology and of our intellect which helps us navigate this very complex world where a lot of things are always changing and where we need to rely on pattern recognition to a certain extent to make quick decisions, especially when it comes down to questions of life and death and survival as such. However, as our societies changed, becoming progressively globalized communities, countries and cities, we became more aware of the entire population of humanity existing. When we think about bias between people, in-group and out-group, this bias is slightly different than our heuristic reflexes. It is where experiences that are directly in front of us make us potentially have a negative predisposition towards other people, or other experiences, because they are different from ours, or because we have been conditioned by our communities, our cultures and our societies to think about things in a certain way. Omitting a lot more complexity, these modes of thinking, as well as our reliance on heuristics, are transferred into the training data that generative models rely on. And this means that as an organization, when you are trying to ensure equal treatment, when you are trying to ensure equity, transparency, clarity of communication, not only is it then more important to be aware of these potential structures and biases with the use of generative artificial intelligence, but also to know how they could potentially transfer over into the data that is subsequently used for models. And that is something that is the responsibility of both developers, but also of the users.

As for the second element, our input and prompts, as individuals, we also need to be aware of our own biases when we are engaging with generative models. Knowing not only where we are positioned as individuals, but also what the strengths and weaknesses of the models are. What can they tell us and what can they cannot. I am using the words ‘tell’, but they provide outputs. We are using excessively humanizing language in a lot of cases when interacting with these models. I worked with artificial intelligence in the military domain and daily our bias comes into our interactions with these models.

Let me better illustrate this point with an example. Imagine this is a question to you, Marianna. If you were to prompt a generative model to give you advice on a decision about whether you should go to war, how would you ask the question?

Marianna: I would list all the motivations why I want to go to war and ask the machine to confirm. I would expect the machine to say that I am right, based on the reasons I listed in my input. And I would expect it to say: ‘You are right. So go to war!’.

Sofia Romansky: Exactly. The way that you ask the question predisposes the model to take on your worldview as correct. If the model was designed to question everything that was said and had its own reference frame, it would not work the way we know it to right now. So it has to take on whatever the user is inputting as true or correct. It will probably say to you that considering these factors, yes, you should go to war because you are assuming that the right thing to do is to go to war because we, as people, also have a war bias. You know, think about theories of international relations, first mover advantage, those kind of things. So that is on the individual level, that is on the input side. When we prompt, it is a question of integrity to be aware of the biases that both our prompt and the model might have and might transfer to the output.

And then finally, on the third element, the output, it might challenge integrity both at the individual and institutional level. Questions like ‘What happens with the outputs? How do we perceive these outputs? Do we accept them automatically? What are our processes to verify and to check?’ It is the responsibility of individuals and of institutions to make sure that we have the systems in place to both benefit from what the models can do and to interrogate ourselves on what kind of questions are we actually asking, but also to still develop knowledge outside of these systems and to not become overly reliant on them.

Because then, and this is the final point that I will bring up for this question, there is another type of bias that comes into the question. Put simply, automation bias is the assumption that because these models have done the difficult processing of potentially massive amounts of data, they will come to an answer that is going to be better than whatever a human can come up with. However, the assumptions about the model are just assumptions.

But because of this bias, this belief that whatever is produced by a machine is more ‘neutral’ and ‘better’ than what a human can produce, we often end up seeing a lot of cognitive offloading, where analysis and thinking that actually allows us to reach good answers as people are handed over to the models.

Therefore, all three elements, the training side, the input side, and the output side are key points where integrity is challenged. And a lot of it has to do with awareness and taking time to think about how these technologies are used. But these technologies, paradoxically, are designed to encourage faster interaction and less thinking. That is the dilemma that we are stuck with.

Sofia Romansky: With generative artificial intelligence specifically, the promised benefit was that we would become much more efficient by having access to a lot of pre-processed information. People would be able to tap into that information and be able to use more time to do other things requiring uniquely human attention. Things that are repetitive and monotonous would be left to the models, and the things that really require attention would be done by humans.

There were also statements about how much time these models would save. For example, now a lot of people use ChatGPT instead of Googling something, because everything you need to know now is supposedly contained within one answer. Users do not have to spend time going through links, identifying which ones are relevant to their query, and which ones are not. On the technical side, these models use something called natural language processing. Natural language processing is a fancy way of saying that they speak the same way that we do. They are speaking in prose, they use expressions like ‘this is what you should consider when you are looking at this and this and this…’.
